title: Book 5 — Terpsichore, Chapter 30
paragraphs: So the Parians had reformed the Milesians. But at the time of which I speak, troubles began to come upon Ionia from these very states, in the following way. From Naxos certain men of the wealthier class were driven into exile by the people, and in their exile they came to Miletus. It happened that Miletus was then under the rule of Aristagoras, son of Molpagoras, who was both son-in-law and cousin of Histiaeus, son of Lysagoras, whom Darius was keeping at Susa. For Histiaeus was tyrant of Miletus, and it happened that he was at Susa at this time when the Naxians came, who had in former times been guest-friends of Histiaeus. When the Naxians arrived, they asked Aristagoras whether he would supply them with a force, so that they might return from exile to their own land. And he, thinking that if they returned to their state through his means he would be ruler of Naxos, but at the same time making a pretext of the guest-friendship with Histiaeus, made them this proposal: “I am not able to promise that I can supply you with force sufficient to bring you back from exile against the will of those Naxians who hold power in the state; for I hear that the Naxians have an army eight thousand shields strong and many warships. But I will use every effort to devise a way; and my plan is this. Artaphrenes happens to be my friend. Now Artaphrenes, you should know, is a son of Hystaspes and brother of King Darius; and he is ruler of all the coastal peoples of Asia, with a great army and many ships. He, I think, will do whatever we ask of him.” Hearing this, the Naxians turned the matter over to Aristagoras to manage as best he could, and they bade him promise gifts and the expenses of the expedition, saying that they would pay them; for they had every expectation that, once they appeared at Naxos, the Naxians would do all their bidding, and likewise the other islanders. For none of these islands, that is to say the Cyclades, was as yet subject to Darius.
